summary: Describes the TCP-based convergence layer protocol for Delay-Tolerant Networking, which carries DTN bundles over TCP connections. It is a product of the IRTF's DTN Research Group and has experimental status.

eli5.summary: Some networks, like ones in space, are slow and often cut off. This document explains how messages for such networks can ride over an ordinary reliable connection.

questions: what is the dtn tcp convergence layer
how does tcpcl shut down a connection
subtitle: How Delay-Tolerant Networking bundles are carried over a TCP connection, with segments, acknowledgments and clean shutdown.

tldr.problem: The Bundle Protocol for delay-tolerant networks needs a convergence layer adapter to send and receive bundles over an ordinary underlying protocol such as TCP.
tldr.mechanism: TCPCL opens a TCP connection, swaps a contact header to negotiate parameters, sends bundles as DATA_SEGMENT messages with optional acknowledgments, refusals and keepalives, and ends with a SHUTDOWN message.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental protocol from the IRTF's DTN Research Group, and it provides no security services of its own.

today: RFC 7242 is an Experimental RFC from the IRTF's DTN Research Group and is not marked as obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It describes version 3 of the TCP convergence-layer protocol.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) is an end-to-end architecture for communicating in stressed environments, with intermittent connectivity, long or variable delays and high bit error rates. Its protocol is the Bundle Protocol (RFC 5050), an application-layer protocol used to build a store-and-forward overlay network.

The Bundle Protocol relies on a convergence-layer adapter to move bundles over some native protocol. This RFC specifies one such adapter that uses TCP, called TCPCL. Both the Bundle Protocol and TCPCL sit at the application layer of the Internet model.

The document defines the format of the protocol data units exchanged by TCPCL peers. It does not cover the Bundle Protocol's own formats or how to locate other bundle nodes. It describes version 3; earlier versions were never publicly specified.
sections.eli5: Bundles are like parcels that wait at each stop until the next road opens. TCPCL is one road, built on a reliable connection, that parcels can ride on.

sections.title: Connection Establishment and the Contact Header
sections.content:
A node first opens a TCP connection to its peer. IANA assigned port 4556 as the well-known port, though other ports MAY be used. If connecting fails, retries MUST wait (a 1-second minimum is RECOMMENDED) and SHOULD use binary exponential backoff.

Once TCP is up, each node MUST immediately send a contact header: the magic bytes dtn!, a version byte (value 3), a flags byte, a two-byte keepalive_interval, and the node's local endpoint identifier (EID) with its length. The flags request acknowledgments, reactive fragmentation, bundle refusal and LENGTH messages.

Negotiation is simple. Acknowledgments and reactive fragmentation are on only if both sides set the flag. Refusal needs acknowledgments to be on. The keepalive interval is the smaller of the two values, and zero from either side disables keepalives. A bad magic string means the connection MUST be terminated. After negotiation, parameters cannot change; the connection must be closed and a new one made.
sections.eli5: When two people meet, they first swap a card saying what they can do, and then agree on the rules both can follow. If anything must change, they hang up and call again.

sections.title: Message Types and Bundle Transfer
sections.content:
After the contact header, every message starts with a one-byte header holding a 4-bit type and 4 flag bits. The types are DATA_SEGMENT (0x1), ACK_SEGMENT (0x2), REFUSE_BUNDLE (0x3), KEEPALIVE (0x4), SHUTDOWN (0x5) and LENGTH (0x6).

A bundle is sent as one or more data segments. Each carries a length (a Self-Delimiting Numeric Value) and that many bytes of bundle data. The S flag marks the first segment of a bundle and the E flag marks the last. Segment size is up to the implementation, and a single segment MUST NOT contain data from more than one bundle. Bundles are sent consecutively; interleaving segments of different bundles is not allowed.

The connection is symmetric: both sides can send bundles at the same time, and acknowledgments may be interleaved with data segments.
sections.eli5: A big parcel is cut into pieces, and each piece gets a label saying how long it is. The first piece is marked START and the last is marked END.

sections.title: Acknowledgments, Refusals and Keepalives
sections.content:
TCP is reliable, but the sender cannot tell when the receiving application has processed data. So TCPCL offers optional acknowledgments. If both sides enabled them, the receiver MUST send an ACK_SEGMENT for each segment, carrying the cumulative length received so far, always ending on a segment boundary. With segments of 100, 200, 500 and 1000 bytes, the acknowledgments are 100, 300, 800 and 1800. Senders can pipeline segments without waiting. There is no explicit flow control at the TCPCL layer. The point is that after a break the sender can use reactive fragmentation instead of resending everything.

A receiver may send REFUSE_BUNDLE with a reason code (0x0 unknown, 0x1 complete bundle already received, 0x2 resources exhausted, 0x3 retransmit entirely). The sender MUST finish any partly sent segment but MUST NOT start further segments of that bundle. The optional LENGTH message tells the receiver a bundle's total size before it starts, so it can refuse early.

KEEPALIVE messages are one byte. Both sides SHOULD send one when the negotiated interval passes with no traffic, and either side MAY end the session if nothing is received for twice the interval.
sections.eli5: Each time you receive a piece, you tell the sender how much you have so far. If you already own the parcel, you can say no thanks. If the line goes quiet for too long, you check that the other side is still there.

sections.title: Connection Termination
sections.content:
To close cleanly, a node sends a SHUTDOWN message after completing any other message. With acknowledgments on, it SHOULD first acknowledge all received data segments. After sending SHUTDOWN a node may still send acknowledgments or refusals but no more data segments.

SHUTDOWN can carry an optional one-byte reason code (0x00 idle timeout, 0x01 version mismatch, 0x02 busy) when the R flag is set, and an optional reconnection delay in seconds when the D flag is set. A delay of 0 means the peer MUST NOT reconnect. A node can also use SHUTDOWN to refuse a connection right after the contact header exchange. If a connection must be dropped in the middle of a message, the node MUST NOT send SHUTDOWN, because the peer might read it as part of the data; it just closes the TCP connection.
sections.eli5: Before hanging up, you say goodbye, and you can add why and how long the other person should wait before calling back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TCPCL provides no security services of its own. A node announces its endpoint identifier in the contact header, and that value could be faked, so a node SHALL NOT use it to derive a peer's identity unless it can verify it by other means. The RFC points to the Bundle Security Protocol (RFC 6257) and notes that nothing prevents using TLS on the connection.

Denial of service is also possible: a node can flood a peer with data or keep reconnecting. A listening node MAY respond by ignoring TCP SYN messages, closing connections quickly, delaying the contact header or sending SHUTDOWN. The RFC also says that if the protocol is used on the Internet, IETF standard protocols for security and congestion control should be used.
sections.eli5: Anyone can say they are someone else on the phone, so you should check by another way. A pest who calls over and over can simply be ignored or hung up on.
